extracted.intended_audience: IP attorneys, in‑house counsel and IP managers handling patent and trademark prosecution and litigation in Latin America (Argentina, Uruguay)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and country‑specific legal standards for prosecuting and litigating patents and trademarks in Latin American jurisdictions (examples: Argentina, Uruguay). Covers patentability, claim drafting, formalities, oppositions, enforcement, remedies and trademark registration/invalidity rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant regulations (patents/trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant treaties and conventions governing IP in the jurisdiction (examples: Paris Convention, TRIPs Agreement) and national statutes and implementing decrees (e.g., Argentine Patent Law N° 24,481 and Regulations, Trademark Law N° 22,362; Uruguayan Patent and TM laws and implementing decrees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and comply with the applicable international treaties incorporated into national law and the cited national laws and official resolutions when preparing filings and strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions of products or processes are patentable provided that they are new, involve an inventive activity (inventive step) and are applicable in industry (industrial applicability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing patentability, evaluate novelty (not in state of the art), inventive step (not obvious to a person skilled in the art) and industrial applicability. Some statutory exclusions (e.g., surgical/therapeutic/diagnostic methods applicable to humans/animals, methods for intellectual activities, games, commercial activities, and certain biological processes) must be considered when drafting claims for filings in Argentina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model eligibility and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models protect tools/devices/objects with a new form that provides an improvement in function; required to be new and industrially applicable but not required to have an inventive step; term is 10 years from application date. Patent applications can be converted to utility model applications and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider converting to or from utility model when inventive step is weak but new form gives functional improvement; check term and local practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software patents and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Software 'per se' is not patentable (protected by copyright). However, claims comprising embedded software in a system or in a specific step of a method are usually accepted; computer‑readable medium claims are not allowed. Means‑plus‑function claims are not allowable as main claims if there are no prior apparatus or method claims. Some examiners may be stricter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft software‑related claims as apparatus or method claims tied to technical features; avoid computer‑readable medium main claims and be prepared to support means‑plus‑function with apparatus/method fallback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush and chemical claim practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Markush claims are accepted provided there is enough support in the specification for the claimed compounds; chemical compounds can be claimed by developed structural formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adequate specification support for genus/Markush groups to withstand examination; include representative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological material deposit and disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention involves biological material not publicly available at filing, a deposit in a recognized depositary (Budapest Treaty IDA accepted) is required; accession data and depositary name/country should be provided at filing; a copy of the deposit should be filed within 90 days of filing in Argentina. The specification must enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the invention; AR PTO may request additional origin/technical information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing biological inventions, arrange deposits early, include deposit/accession details, and ensure the specification contains reproduction steps or references to the deposit. Be prepared to supplement information on request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linkage system (pharma)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no linkage system in Argentina (i.e., no regulatory approval linkage between patent status and marketing authorizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on drug regulatory linkage mechanisms for enforcement strategies in Argentina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and inventive step definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty: invention not included in the state of the art (all public technical knowledge before filing or priority date). Inventive step: invention not obvious or evidently deduced from the prior art to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform clearance and inventive step analyses against the full state of the art (published descriptions, uses, disclosures worldwide) before filing or prosecuting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting: clarity, structure and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should define the invention; first claim should be independent and include relevant features; dependent claims subordinate. No limit on number of claims, but official fees apply for claims in excess of the 10th. Claims must have support in the specification as filed; new subject matter cannot be added at any stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a clear independent first claim, well‑supported dependent claims, and manage claim count to control fees. Avoid introducing new matter in amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting: AR PTO 'Characterized' format
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be characterized to adapt to AR PTO practice: a first part describing prior art features and a 'Characterized' part detailing the relevant novel features claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using the 'characterized in that' format when prosecuting in Argentina to align with Office preferences and improve examiner understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for intellectual activities, games, commercial activities; methods for presenting information; surgical, therapeutic or diagnostic methods applicable to humans and animals are not considered inventions and cannot be protected by patents in Argentina. Biological methods for reproduction and genetic processes may be considered inventions but are excluded from patentability under AR law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drafting claims that would fall squarely into excluded categories when planning filings in Argentina; use alternative claim strategies where appropriate (e.g., device/apparatus or product claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application formalities and required documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Required at filing: applicant and inventor information; Power of Attorney (notarized and apostilled; can be filed within 40 working days if unavailable); title, specification, abstract, drawings (if available), one or more claims; priority information and priority documents (filed within 90 days with sworn Spanish translation); assignment of priority rights (if applicable) filed within 90 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare translators and legalization (Apostille) processes in advance to meet 40‑ and 90‑day formal deadlines; include clear priority data at filing to avoid loss of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority document translation and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority documents must be filed within 90 days of filing the application, with a sworn Spanish translation by an Argentinean registered translator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget time for certified translation and submission of priority documents to avoid priority loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant/POA timing flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If Power of Attorney is not available at the time of filing, it can be filed within 40 working days of filing the application in Argentina (analogous provisions in other jurisdictions may vary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 40‑day window to secure notarization/apostille rather than delay filing; ensure POA is correctly legalized to avoid formal objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent term is 20 years from the AR filing date. The 20‑year term is not extendable; Argentine legislation has not provided for supplementary protection certificates (SPCs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan global patent term strategies accordingly; do not expect SPCs in Argentina.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME filing benefits and fee reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: SME criteria trigger special filing benefits: SMEs pay 50% of the official fees established by AR Patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess applicant SME status to take advantage of reduced official fees where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited or prioritized examination practice
rubrics_metrics.description: AR PTO follows a chronological order for substantive examination set by the date of payment of the examination fee. Requesting substantive examination and paying the fee early speeds prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request and pay for substantive examination promptly to shorten pendency; check for specific prioritized pathways as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition system (pre‑grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argentina provides a pre‑grant opposition system: any person may file objections and documentary proof within 60 days following publication of the patent application; examiners will evaluate the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor publications, be prepared to respond to oppositions, and submit third‑party observations early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner interviews are allowed and have proven helpful in answering office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews to clarify claim scope and address examiner concerns; prepare concise arguments and claim amendments ahead of the interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection provided by pending applications (provisional protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights are enforceable in Argentina only once the patent is granted; there is no enforceability/provisional protection between filing date and grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume enforceable rights during pendency; use cease‑and‑desist letters and prepare for post‑grant enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim amendments timing and new matter prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can voluntarily amend description, claims and drawings during the first 90 days after filing. After that, only amendments requested by the AR PTO examiner or amendments to answer office actions or adapt claims to those granted by a foreign PTO are allowed. New subject matter cannot be incorporated at any stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make substantive edits within the initial 90‑day window; avoid attempts to add new matter later—rely on divisional filings if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary divisional applications are allowed before parent grant. Divisional applications are commonly filed when an examiner raises lack of unity; if requested by the examiner, divisional must be filed within 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider filing voluntary divisionals to preserve claim scope and manage unity objections; track deadlines when examiner requests divisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional applications have not been regulated under Argentine patent legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan filings without reliance on a formal provisional route in Argentina; use priority claims from foreign provisionals where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent infringement standing and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner may bring actions before civil or criminal courts. Licensees may bring civil infringement actions only if the owner does not exercise them. Patent confers exclusive rights to prevent third parties from manufacturing, using, offering for sale, or importing the patented product, and to prevent use of a patented process and products directly obtained by that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm standing before initiating suits; consider civil vs criminal strategies and licensing issues in enforcement planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' technical expertise and use of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are attorneys without technical backgrounds and rely on court‑appointed technical experts to provide reports on infringement and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare strong expert evidence and be ready to work with court‑appointed experts; technical expert reports are crucial to persuade courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation timelines (patent/trademark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent infringement actions at first instance can take 3–5 years; appeals can take 1–2 years. Trademark infringement first instance 2–4 years; appeals 1–2 years. Uruguay and other countries show similar multi‑year timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan enforcement timelines and cash flow for multi‑year litigation; consider alternate dispute resolution where speed is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations on damages claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Damage claims should be initiated within three (3) years from the time of the infringement. For trademarks some regimes allow one year from knowledge in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve evidence and act promptly to file damage claims within statutory limits; document discovery of infringement date to trigger limitation reckoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions and interim reliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Available interim remedies include seizure of infringing goods, inventory/attachment of infringing goods and machines, description of incriminated process, injunctions preventing entry into the market or to preserve evidence (similar to art. 50 TRIPS). Certain preliminary measures (seizure, inventory, description) can be granted ex‑parte; temporary injunctions usually require notice and court expert report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For injunctions similar to TRIPS art. 50, be prepared to prove probable validity of the patent, accept court‑appointed expert involvement, and post required bonds; collect compelling prima facie evidence before seeking ex‑parte measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for granting provisional injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional requirements for TRIPS‑like preliminary measures: (1) proof of reasonable likelihood that the patent will be declared valid if challenged; (2) appointment of an expert ex officio by the court; (3) inaudita altera parte relief only in exceptional cases (risk of evidence destruction); (4) court must balance harm to patent holder against potential harm to alleged infringer. Bonds are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare technical and legal evidence to show likely validity, anticipate court expert scrutiny, quantify harms, and arrange bond funds before filing for injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex‑parte remedies and temporary injunction practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain preliminary measures (seizure, inventory, description) are ex‑parte. Temporary injunctions are not granted ex‑parte and require serving notice to the defendant and a court‑appointed expert report on the requirements for the injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ex‑parte remedies for preservation where permitted, but expect temporary injunctions to require adversarial process and expert reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonds related to interim reliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts require deposit of a bond determined by the court to grant temporary injunctions; preliminary measures may also require bonds. If a temporary injunction is not issued, plaintiff can request the defendant to post a bond if plaintiff intends to continue prosecuting the infringement action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for bonds when seeking interim relief and consider alternative security arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity defenses and counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may assert patent invalidity before the court dealing with the infringement action and must provide evidence that the invention lacks novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability. Assertion of invalidity may lead to a judge declaring the patent invalid or confirming its validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare robust validity evidence both for plaintiffs (to defend against invalidity) and defendants (to attack patents); consider separate nullity actions if procedural bifurcation makes unity difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and pre‑trial procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no discovery as in U.S. practice. Pre‑trial preliminary measures to preserve evidence or obtain documents can be requested from the judge. Mediation is a mandatory pretrial procedure in Argentina before filing a lawsuit (but not required to request a temporary injunction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available preservation and evidence‑gathering preliminary measures early; comply with mandatory mediation steps where required before filing infringement suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof (product vs process patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: For product patents, burden of proof lies on the patent owner. For process patents, courts may order the defendant to prove that the process to obtain an identical product is different from the patented process (per TRIPS article 34/AR law). Courts may require the plaintiff to prove use of the patented process if defendant proves availability of identical product, existence at the time of infringement, and that the product is obtainable by different means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather evidence demonstrating literal or equivalent use for product claims; for process patents plan to invoke statutory presumptions and prepare technical evidence to show process identity or difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert evidence and technical proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges rely mainly on opinions from court‑appointed technical experts and on documents from official/private institutions. Expert reports and technical tests are central evidence in infringement and nullity proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure credible technical experts, prepare reproducible tests and documentation, and anticipate court expert methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness evidence practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Witness depositions are not usually proposed; commonly submitted evidence includes documents, technical expert reports, technical tests and questionnaires answered by institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on documentary and expert proof rather than witness testimony; assemble invoices, shipping records, advertisements and laboratory test results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages and litigation costs; bond and fee shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: Punitive damages are not provided. Before final decision, courts may demand a plaintiff deposit a bond equivalent to 3% of the amount requested as compensation for damages. Losing party must pay the prevailing party's attorneys' fees, typically set by the judge between 11% and 20% of the damages claimed. If no money amount is involved, judges fix fees considering complexity and duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in bonds and potential fee‑shifting exposure when deciding to litigate; quantify realistic damages requests mindful of bond percentage and likely attorneys’ fee awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate practice and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals from first instance to federal appeals have short filing windows (e.g., five working days to file appeal, then five days to ground the appeal; Supreme Court appeals for constitutional issues within ten working days). Procedures are written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare rapid appellate filings and written grounds within strict timeframes; keep appellate evidence and arguments ready in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement, mediation and ADR
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation proceedings are a mandatory step in Argentina before filing a lawsuit. Arbitration is not regularly used for IP matters in Argentina and Uruguay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in mediation early as required by procedure; consider arbitration only where parties contractually agree or in jurisdictions more favorable to ADR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: No personal liability for corporate executives in civil proceedings; individuals may face criminal liability (fines and imprisonment, e.g., six months to three years in Argentina) if criminal proceedings are pursued and guilt is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider criminal exposure only in jurisdictions/industries where prosecutors pursue IP crimes; corporate defense strategies should address both civil and potential criminal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust considerations in enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants may use patent or trademark enforcement actions to complain to antitrust authorities; experience shows complaints may be filed though precedents are limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess antitrust risk of enforcement strategies (e.g., preliminary injunctions or exclusionary remedies) and prepare economic/competition law justifications to mitigate antitrust complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of trademarks registrable
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominative, figurative, combined, three‑dimensional, and non‑traditional marks (audible, olfactory, taste and others) can be registered provided they have distinctive capacity; representation issues for non‑traditional marks may arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing non‑traditional marks, ensure feasible representation for publication and consider technical limitations for Office searching and management (e.g., sound file storage only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unregistrable marks (absolute grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs that are necessary or habitual designation of the product/service, descriptive, become generic, lack distinctiveness, induce error about nature/quality/origin, offend public morality, include official insignia or names without consent, pseudonyms/portraits without consent, or advertising phrases lacking originality cannot be registered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct distinctiveness and descriptiveness clearance and avoid marks that are purely descriptive or generic; secure consents when using personal names/portraits or official emblems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famous and well‑known mark protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Famous and well‑known marks are protected according to Paris Convention and TRIPS and national statutes and supported by judicial precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with famous marks, consider broader protection and opposition/invalidity strategies even across non‑identical classes based on notoriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Although exclusive rights are achieved through registration, judicial precedent can recognize rights based on prior legal, continuous and visible use; proprietors of unregistered marks may have the right to oppose similar applications if they can prove use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document continuous use and gather evidence (invoices, advertising) to assert prior user rights; monitor filings to oppose conflicting applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indications and appellations
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical indications and appellations of origin are registrable under specific national laws (e.g., Law N° 25,163 for wines/spirits in Argentina; UY law provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specific statutory routes for GI protection rather than standard trademark filings when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness and confusing similarity criteria (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks must not be visually, phonetically or ideologically similar. Other factors: type of consumer, fame of marks, prior market coexistence, common ingredients, orthography, figures, colors, shapes, and overall commercial impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform multi‑factor similarity analysis (visual/phonetic/conceptual + consumer sophistication + fame + coexistence) when clearing marks or litigating. Consider evidence of confusion and consumer surveys where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark application formalities and priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Each class requires an application including applicant’s name/address, trademark description, list of goods/services, priority country and number (priority certificate within 90 days), and Power of Attorney (notarized and apostilled; timeframe for filing varies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File a separate application per class as required or use multiclass where accepted (e.g., Uruguay accepts multiclass); submit priority documents and legalized POA within statutory timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark pre‑grant opposition period
rubrics_metrics.description: Argentina and Uruguay provide pre‑grant opposition systems. Argentina: 30 days following publication to file opposition on trademark applications. Uruguay: similar pre‑grant opposition procedures (30 days or per Office practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor the official gazette and file oppositions within the 30‑day window if rights are threatened; prepare opposition evidence and arguments early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection during pendency of trademark applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark rights are enforceable only after grant; the only right derived from an application during pendency is the priority right to file in third countries claiming priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume enforceability during pendency; send cease‑and‑desist letters and prepare for enforcement post‑grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution delays (trademark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Average prosecution term without opposition: Argentina ~14–18 months; with opposition longer. Uruguay: up to 18 months without opposition and up to 36 months with oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate multi‑year prosecution and monitor opposition responses to manage timelines and client expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name registration and conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain names are registered with a national registrar (e.g., NIC Argentina). Registration is generally first‑come, first‑served; procedures exist to challenge domain registrations conflicting with trademarks. Terms typically one year renewable. In Uruguay domain registration processes and criteria may be less formal and limited to identical name existence checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register domain names proactively and monitor national registries; use administrative challenge procedures if domain registration conflicts with trademark rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews for trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner interviews are allowed (Argentina) and helpful to overcome office actions. In some jurisdictions (Uruguay) there may be no provision for examiner interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews where available to clarify registrability issues and propose amendments or evidence of distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark enforcement remedies and interim reliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners may request embargo, inventory and description of goods, seizure of infringing products, injunctions to prevent market entry or preserve evidence (TRIPS art.50‑type measures). Remedies are often ex‑parte and require bonds; revocation/appeal mechanisms exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to seek interim measures with documentary and expert evidence, arrange bonds, and coordinate reliefs with nullity/administrative proceedings where bifurcation may occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark criminal sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions (e.g., Uruguay) provide criminal penalties for trademark infringement, including imprisonment (three months up to six years) in certain cases (e.g., refilling original containers, knowing marketing of infringing products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider criminal complaints where strategic and evidentiary thresholds met; coordinate civil and criminal strategies carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark infringement actions can be started while the infringing mark is in the market; there may be limitations (e.g., Uruguay: not after four years from infringement or one year from owner’s knowledge; Argentina: three years for damages claims or one year from knowledge in some cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document discovery dates of infringement and act promptly to preserve civil and criminal remedies within limitation periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark invalidity and bifurcated procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Nullity/invalidity actions may be filed administratively (before the TM Office or administrative courts) while infringement actions proceed in civil/criminal courts; bifurcation can make simultaneous resolution difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate invalidity and infringement strategies, recognizing possible procedural bifurcation and differing timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee shifting in IP litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The losing party is generally obliged to pay the prevailing party's attorney fees as determined by the judge (percentages or judge‑set amounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess litigation risk including likely fee awards and include potential fee exposure in settlement negotiations.
